svg.title: Sigstore keyless signing architecture and the xz-utils case study
svg.desc: Three component panels and a case study. Fulcio authenticates via OpenID Connect and issues an ephemeral X.509 certificate valid for about ten minutes, binding the public key to the verified workload identity and removing long-lived key management. Rekor is an append-only, tamper-evident Merkle transparency log that stores the signature, certificate and artifact digest and returns an inclusion proof against a co-signed checkpoint; Rekor v2 no longer issues Signed Entry Timestamps, so clients obtain an RFC 3161 timestamp from a timestamp authority. Cosign signs container images and blobs, stores signatures as OCI artifacts, and verifies the certificate identity, with Kubernetes admission controllers enforcing the policy. The case study panel records that in xz-utils the payload test fixtures were present in Git while only the modified build-to-host.m4 shipped in the release tarball, that the maintainer account was earned rather than stolen, and that signing proves who produced an artifact but not that its contents are safe.
svg.text: Keyless signing via Fulcio short-lived certificates, the Rekor transparency log, Cosign, and the xz-utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094).

REAL-WORLD CASE STUDY: THE XZ-UTILS BACKDOOR (CVE-2024-3094)
Release Tarball Divergence vs Source Code Audit
• Mechanism: the payload test fixtures were committed openly in Git; only the modified m4/build-to-host.m4 shipped in the release tarball
• Access: the maintainer account was earned over roughly two years, not stolen — no credential control would have prevented it
• Lesson: signing proves *who* produced an artifact; it does not prove the contents are safe. Build the tarball from the tagged commit.
SIGSTORE FLOW: OIDC AUTHENTICATION → FULCIO CERTIFICATE → COSIGN SIGNING → REKOR LOGGING → RFC 3161 TIMESTAMP
